newsitem.title: USA: GM strikes pushing market share goals out of reach.
newsitem.headline: GM strikes pushing market share goals out of reach.

text.p: General Motors Corp. is making some progress in its bid to win new car and truck customers but strikes probably will stop it from reaching its goal of capturing 33 percent of the U.S. market, Chairman Jack Smith said Thursday.

Smith, speaking to reporters at GM's new headquarters in Detroit, also said it would be difficult for the world's largest automaker to complete the spinoff of 20 percent of its Delphi Automotive Systems parts unit by year-end.

In addition, he said GM's mid-size car venture in Shanghai, China, may not start volume production until April 1999 -- four months late -- because of prolonged negotiations to win final approval from the Chinese government.
In 1996, GM captured about 31 percent of the U.S. car and truck market and had hoped that several new car models this year would reverse a long-term slide in its market share.

"I think we're going to do better than last year, but obviously we're not going to be at the upper limits of what we thought we'd be able to do," Smith said. "It would be tough to hit the 33 percent number with the strikes."
He said a seven-week strike in Oklahoma City has sharply cut supplies of GM's new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass mid-sized models, adding GM cannot make up that lost production this year.

The Oklahoma City strike and a 37-day-old walkout at GM's Pontiac, Mich., pickup truck plant will significantly dent GM's May sales, holding them below the 482,312 units sold in the unusually strong month of May 1996, Smith said.

Burnham Securities analyst David Healy said he thought stiffer competition from Japanese automakers was a bigger reason for GM's market share woes and was blunting the positive impact of GM's new car models.

"The older models are slipping away as fast as the newer ones are coming on-stream," Healy said. He estimated GM's market share for the first five months of 1997 at 30.5 percent, compared with 31.6 percent a year earlier.

GM tentatively settled the Oklahoma strike on Sunday by agreeing to hire about 300 new workers at the plant. Smith said the pact "pretty much" maintains recent productivity gains at the factory and allows the Cutlass and Malibu to remain cost-competitive cars.
But Smith said GM won't settle the Pontiac strike without obtaining competitive staffing levels in the truck plant.
"I think we've got plants that aren't as competitive as they need to be. We've got a strong push to get those plants competitive," he said.

On the Delphi spinoff, Smith said the transaction must follow the $9.5 billion sale of GM's Hughes Electronics Corp. defence operations to Raytheon Co., which is not expected to be completed until the fourth quarter.
"It would be a big challenge to get it done this year," he said of the Delphi spinoff.

Smith and GM Vice Chairman Harry Pearce said the Delphi deal, which may take the form of an initial public offering, would also have to follow the consolidation of Hughes' Delco Electronics unit into Delphi. Delco, which makes automotive electronics parts, is not being sold to Raytheon.
GM is awaiting rulings on tax and antitrust issues related to the Hughes-Raytheon deal and expects those matters to be resolved favourably, Pearce said.

Smith also said GM had completed about 70 percent of a $2.5 billion stock buyback programme. He declined to say whether losses from the strikes would affect GM's ability to launch future buyback programmes. Through May 15, GM said the strikes had reduced second quarter net income by about $225 million.
"At the moment, we are continuing to complete the buyback that we started," Smith said.

Regarding the Shanghai venture, Smith said GM probably does not have enough time to complete construction of the plant to meet the previously scheduled launch of December 1998 since winning final approval has taken longer than expected.
"Internally, we're saying April of 1999," he said.

GM and Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp. will each own 50 percent of the $1 billion joint venture, called Shanghai General Motors Corp. It will eventually have capacity to produce 100,000 Buick Regal sedans a year.
Smith also said that denial of U.S. most favoured nation trade privileges for China would hurt U.S. companies and simply push China to do business with foreign firms.
"You'd cut off the U.S. economic opportunity with China, he said. "I don't think that's wise."
GM stock fell $1 to $56.75 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
